neighbors.heading: one mouthful
neighbors.text: Today a hymn walked a whole life through four watches of the night, and asked which watch it is now. Buddhists ask that too. The Buddha once asked his monks how often they thought of death. One said, for a day; another, for a meal. He praised the two who said: for one mouthful, and for one breath in and out.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the merchant friend is called back to the Name before the night ends. Buddhists don't turn to a God here; remembering death spurs practice, letting go of clinging while there is time.
neighbors.shared: this hour is the one we're given.

neighbors.heading: number our days
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak sang a life in four watches of the night, and asked which watch it is now. Christians pray that question too. A psalm asks God: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." And Jesus told of a rich man building bigger barns, who didn't know his life would be asked of him that night.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs answer the passing night with remembrance of the Name. Christians number their days in hope of resurrection and life with God through Christ.
neighbors.shared: a short life is a reason to wake up, not to fear.

neighbors.heading: seeing the better
neighbors.text: Today a Guru admitted the mind won't do what it's told, and kept going, gently. People on their own path know that sentence. The Roman poet Ovid gave Medea a line still quoted: I see the better way and approve it, and I follow the worse. One study found that meeting a slip with kindness, not scolding, helped people try again.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the stubborn mind is turned by remembering the Name each day. Ovid and the study offer no God; the turning comes from honest self-knowledge, patience and practice.
neighbors.shared: slipping back isn't the end; you begin again, gently.
neighbors.sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.20–21 (paraphrase) · Breines and Chen, "Self-Compassion Increases Self-Improvement Motivation" (2012) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good which i will
neighbors.text: Today a Guru said the mind won't listen, however often it's taught. Catholics hear Saint Paul say the same: "For the good which I will, I do not; but the evil which I will not, that I do." Paul doesn't end in despair; he ends in thanks for grace. Catholics bring that same struggle to confession, again and again.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the stubborn mind is steadied by remembering the Name. For Catholics, the struggle is a wound left by original sin, healed by Christ's grace, especially in the sacraments.
neighbors.shared: an honest "i keep slipping" is already a kind of prayer.

neighbors.heading: by that light
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak made the sky an aarti tray, with the sun and moon for lamps. Hindus, who wave the lamp at home and in temple, know that turn too. An Upanishad says the sun does not shine there, nor the moon and stars; when the One shines, everything shines after, and all this is lit by that light.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, the lamp waved before a sacred image is a loving offering in itself. Guru Nanak's hymn sets the tray aside: the whole universe is already performing the aarti.
neighbors.shared: every light you see can turn your heart to its source.

neighbors.heading: the heavens declare
neighbors.text: Today the whole sky became an aarti: sun and moon the lamps, stars the pearls. Jews sing a sky like that. A psalm says: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth His handiwork." Another calls on creation itself: "Praise ye Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all ye stars of light."
neighbors.difference: In the Sikh hymn, the sky is already worshiping, so no lamp needs lighting. In Judaism, the heavens' praise sits beside commanded acts, like Shabbat candles lit by hand for the God of Israel.
neighbors.shared: look up tonight; the sky is already praising.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 19:2 and Psalm 148:3 (JPS 1917; Psalm 19:1 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: without me
neighbors.text: Today a morning hymn began with plain need: without the Lord, my mind cannot live. Christians hear Jesus say it from the other side: "I am the vine, ye are the branches... for without me ye can do nothing." And the first blessing in his Sermon on the Mount goes to need: "Blessed are the poor in spirit."
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the Guru brings the seeker to meet the Lord, the breath of life. For Christians, Jesus himself is the vine, God made flesh, and the branches live by staying in him.
neighbors.shared: admitting you need help is where strength begins.

neighbors.heading: ye are the poor
neighbors.text: Today a morning raga opened by admitting need, no armor on yet. Muslims start the day the same way, rising before the sun for the dawn prayer, Fajr. The Qur'an names the need plainly: "O mankind! Ye are the poor in your relation to Allah. And Allah! He is the Absolute, the Owner of Praise."
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the Lord is the beloved breath, met through the Guru. Muslims turn to Allah directly in set prayers five times a day, and Allah, who needs nothing, is never described as needing us back.
neighbors.shared: admitting you need help is where strength begins.

neighbors.heading: a clean heart
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak washed the pot before the milk went in. Catholics pray for a clean vessel too. A psalm asks: "Create a clean heart in me, O God: and renew a right spirit within my bowels." Before Communion, Catholics examine their conscience, and confess serious sin first, readying the vessel to receive.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the cleaning is a daily discipline of good deeds and the Name. Catholics believe the heart is made clean by God's grace in confession, and what they receive is Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: wash the pot first; something good is on its way.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 50:12 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 51:10 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1385 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: purify the mind
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak washed the pot first, then brought the milk, and churned with patience. Buddhists start there too. A verse of the Dhammapada sums up the whole teaching: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the clean vessel is made ready for the one Name and union with the Lord. Buddhists purify the mind by their own practice, to be free of craving, not to meet a creator God.
neighbors.shared: make room inside before you ask for something new.

neighbors.heading: a weaned child
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak stepped out of the lineup of the learned: I know nothing; I know only your Name. Jews sing a psalm of the same calm: "neither do I exercise myself in things too great, or in things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother."
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak rests in the one Name through the Guru's Word. Jews sing this psalm before the God of Israel, and still prize hard study of Torah; there, humility and learning walk together.
neighbors.shared: saying "i don't know" can be the calmest sentence of the day.

neighbors.heading: i neither know
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak didn't compete with the scholars; he said, I know nothing. People on their own path honor that move. In Plato's Apology, Socrates questions a man famed for wisdom and walks away thinking: "I neither know nor think that I know." For Socrates, that honest not-knowing was where wisdom starts.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak's not-knowing rests in the one Name and asks the Lord's kindness. Socrates' not-knowing keeps him asking questions; it leans on reason and examination rather than devotion.
neighbors.shared: saying "i don't know" can be the calmest sentence of the day.

neighbors.heading: the devotion reacheth him
neighbors.text: Today Namdev brought a cup of milk, and what reached the Lord was his heart. Muslims hear the same at Eid al-Adha. The Qur'an says of the sacrifice: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." The meat is shared with family, neighbors and the poor.
neighbors.difference: In Namdev's hymn, the Lord smiles and drinks the milk. Muslims hold that Allah needs nothing and takes no food; the offering feeds people, and the devotion is what rises to Him.
neighbors.shared: what reaches heaven is the heart you carry it in.

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today Namdev carried a cup of milk and begged the Lord to drink. Hindus know that cup; Namdev is still sung as a saint in Maharashtra's Varkari tradition. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with devotion, he accepts, given in love.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus offer food before a sacred image, then share it as prasad, a blessing. Sikhs read Namdev's cup, placed in the Granth, as devotion to the One beyond form, met without images.
neighbors.shared: what reaches heaven is the heart you carry it in.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (paraphrase) · Namdev in the Varkari tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one great cloud
neighbors.text: Today rain fell on every field, and a leather worker's son was honored. Buddhists tell a rain story too: in the Lotus Sutra, one great cloud rains on every plant alike, and each grows in its own way. And in an older sutta, the Buddha says no one is low or noble by birth, only by deeds.
neighbors.difference: Ravidas is lifted by the Lord's Name, a grace from beyond him. For Buddhists, the rain is the Buddha's teaching, and freedom comes by walking the path oneself, without a creator God.
neighbors.shared: the rain falls on every field alike.
neighbors.sources: Lotus Sutra, chapter 5, the parable of the plants (paraphrase) · Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rain on the just
neighbors.text: Today the rain fell on every field, and a leather worker's son was honored for the Name. Jesus pointed at the same sky: God "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." And Peter, in a Roman officer's home, said: "God is no respecter of persons."
neighbors.difference: Ravidas is honored through the Name, his hymns sung beside the Gurus' own. Christians speak of grace given in Christ, gathering a church where birth and rank don't decide your seat.
neighbors.shared: grace doesn't check your family name first.

neighbors.heading: nothing human is foreign
neighbors.text: Today a Guru said: no one is my enemy, no one is a stranger. People on their own path reach for an old line. The Roman playwright Terence gave a character the words still quoted: I am human, so nothing human is foreign to me. Philosophers since have taken it as a whole way of meeting people.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, strangers vanish because the One is present in everyone, seen in holy company. Terence's line asks for no belief in God; it rests on shared humanity alone.
neighbors.shared: the person at the next table is not a stranger.

neighbors.heading: who is my neighbour
neighbors.text: Today a Guru said: no one is my enemy, no one a stranger. Catholics hear Jesus push the same way: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you." And when a lawyer asked, "who is my neighbour?", Jesus told of a Samaritan, a foreigner, who stopped for a wounded man on the road.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, jealousy falls away in holy company and the One is seen in all. Catholics love even enemies because Christ commanded it, seeing each person as made in God's image, and lean on grace to do it.
neighbors.shared: no one is a stranger once you've really seen them.

neighbors.heading: a lotus leaf
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak pointed to a lotus and a duck: in the water all day, never soaked. Hindus know the lotus picture well. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says one who acts without clinging, offering every act to the divine, is untouched, like a lotus leaf by water. And he told Arjuna to stay and act, not run away.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus also honor the renouncer, the sannyasi, as a holy path and stage of life. Guru Nanak pointed the yogis back to the household as the place to live untouched.
neighbors.shared: you can be in the water and still stay dry.

neighbors.heading: torah and a trade
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak told the yogis you don't have to leave the stream to stay dry. Jewish teaching also keeps holiness inside ordinary life. In Pirkei Avot, a sage says Torah study is best joined with a worldly trade, because the effort of both keeps wrongdoing out of mind. A home, a table, a job: there the commandments are kept.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, staying untouched comes from keeping the One Name settled in the mind. For Jews, it comes through living Torah's commandments, given to Israel, in every part of the day.
neighbors.shared: holiness can live at a kitchen table, not only a mountaintop.

neighbors.heading: put on kindness
neighbors.text: Today the yogis offered Nanak their earrings and coat, and he chose to wear the Word inside. Christians are told to dress the same way: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering." An older verse says: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."
neighbors.difference: Many Sikhs keep outward articles too, like the turban and the Five Ks, with the Word within. For Christians, the deepest clothing is Christ himself: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ."
neighbors.shared: what you wear inside is the part people feel.

neighbors.heading: the raiment of restraint
neighbors.text: Today Nanak traded the yogis' earrings for the Word worn within. The Qur'an speaks of clothing the same way: "We have revealed unto you raiment to conceal your shame, and splendid vesture, but the raiment of restraint from evil, that is best." A hadith adds that Allah looks not at your bodies or faces, but at your hearts.
neighbors.difference: Muslims keep outward signs too, like modest dress and the set movements of prayer, as obedience to Allah's revealed law. Many Sikhs wear the Five Ks, and Nanak taught the Word as the earring no one sees.
neighbors.shared: the best clothes are the ones nobody sees.

neighbors.heading: with modesty
neighbors.text: Today Nanak answered the yogis' hard questions without mocking them. Catholics are asked to answer that way: "being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you. But with modesty and fear." The Church also teaches that it rejects nothing true and holy in other religions.
neighbors.difference: Nanak answered from the Word, turning the yogis' own terms toward the Name. Catholics enter dialogue honoring what is true in others, while proclaiming Christ as the way, the truth and the life.
neighbors.shared: you can disagree and still leave the other person heard.

neighbors.heading: well-spoken words
neighbors.text: Today Nanak met pointed questions with patient answers, never mockery. Buddhists call that skill right speech. The Buddha said well-spoken words have five marks: spoken at the right time, true, gentle, helpful, and said with goodwill. He too often met other teachers in conversation, taking up their words and giving them new meaning.
neighbors.difference: Nanak turned the yogis' words toward the one Name and the Guru's Word. The Buddha turned old words, like brahmin or the sacred fire, toward his path of awakening, without a creator God.
neighbors.shared: a kind answer can carry a hard truth.

neighbors.heading: study and doing
neighbors.text: Today the pandit read and argued, but had he understood? Jews prize study deeply, and still ask that question. In Pirkei Avot, a sage says: not study but doing is the main thing. And when the rabbis debated which is greater, study or deeds, they answered study, because it leads to doing.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the treasure is the Name within, which reading alone can miss. In Judaism, Torah study is itself a commandment and a form of worship, and it bears fruit in keeping the commandments.
neighbors.shared: the best reading is the one that changes how you live.

neighbors.heading: for life, not for school
neighbors.text: Today the pandit could quote every page and still miss the treasure inside him. People on their own path have said this a long time. Seneca complained that we learn for the classroom, not for life. And Montaigne wrote that we labor to stuff the memory, and leave understanding and conscience empty.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak points the reader to the Name, the treasure within. Seneca and Montaigne point to wisdom lived out, a good life built on reason and character, which needs no belief in God.
neighbors.shared: a full shelf isn't the same as a changed heart.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters 106 (paraphrase) · Montaigne, Essays I.25, "Of Pedantry" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what he did with it
neighbors.text: Today the Patti said you're truly read only when you can give an account of your life. Muslims hear the same test. A hadith says that on the Last Day each person is asked about their life, how they spent it, and about their knowledge, what they did with it. The Prophet prayed for refuge from knowledge that does not benefit.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, learning shows in seeing the One in all and letting go of "I, I." For Muslims, beneficial knowledge is lived in obedience to Allah, and the account is given on a Day of Judgment.
neighbors.shared: what you know is measured by what you do with it.

neighbors.heading: the higher knowledge
neighbors.text: Today the Patti said reading isn't the finish line. Hindus have a famous version. In the Mundaka Upanishad, a teacher says there are two kinds of knowledge. The lower is the Vedas themselves, with grammar and the other learned arts. The higher is the knowledge by which the Imperishable is known.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the higher knowledge comes through a teacher and meditation on Brahman, the Imperishable. In the Patti, it comes through the Guru's Word and the Name, and shows in a humble life.
neighbors.shared: the letters are a door; living them is walking through.

neighbors.heading: the world is burning
neighbors.text: Today the summer burned, and the bride felt the heat of being apart. Buddhists name that heat honestly. In his first teaching, the Buddha said being separated from what we love is suffering. He also spoke of the whole world burning, with craving, aversion and confusion, and of the freedom that comes when that fire goes out.
neighbors.difference: In the Barah Maha, the cure for the heat is nearness to the Beloved, God. For Buddhists, the cooling comes from letting go of craving itself, not from meeting a God.
neighbors.shared: it's honest to say it: being apart hurts.
neighbors.sources: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 (paraphrase) · Adittapariyaya Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a dry and thirsty land
neighbors.text: Today the earth burned, and the bride, apart from her Beloved, prayed and looked for shade. Christians pray from that same heat. A psalm says: "my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is." Another calls the LORD "thy shade upon thy right hand."
neighbors.difference: In the Barah Maha, the longing is a bride's for the Beloved, met through the Name. Christians pray these psalms as longing for God, answered in Christ, who promised "living water."
neighbors.shared: the thirst itself can be a kind of prayer.

neighbors.heading: love made visible
neighbors.text: Today the story of Lalo's plain bread made honest work part of the path. People on their own path say this too. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran writes: "Work is love made visible." And: "if you bake bread with indifference, you bake a bitter bread that feeds but half man's hunger."
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak ties honest work to remembering the Name and giving from your hand. Gibran's prophet speaks of love and life, not a set path or God's command; readers take him as they choose.
neighbors.shared: what you make with care feeds more than hunger.

neighbors.heading: working with his hands
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said the one who earns by effort and gives from his hand knows the path. Catholics read almost the same: "let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have something to give to him that suffereth need." Saint Benedict's Rule calls idleness the enemy of the soul.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, honest work stands beside remembering the Name and sharing. For Catholics, work shares in God's creating and in Christ's own years as a carpenter, offered up to God.
neighbors.shared: honest hands and an open hand belong together.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 4:28 (Douay-Rheims) · Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 48 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: You are the form of light

neighbors.heading: know the self
neighbors.text: Today a Guru told the mind: you are the form of light; know your origin. Hindus know that call. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the living self in every being is an eternal part of him. And in an Upanishad, a sage tells his wife that when the true Self is seen and known, all this is known.
neighbors.difference: Hindu schools differ: some hold the true Self is one with Brahman, others that the soul stays forever distinct, serving God. The Guru says you are light, so seek the Lord who is its source.
neighbors.shared: underneath the noise, there is light in you.

neighbors.heading: the lamp of the lord
neighbors.text: Today a Guru told the mind it is a form of light, and to know where it came from. Jews have a lamp verse too: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." And Genesis tells how God breathed the breath of life into the first human, made in God's own image.
neighbors.difference: The Guru speaks of the mind as light from the One, seeking its source. In Judaism, the soul is God's lamp, a gift from its Maker, and its light is lived by keeping Torah's commandments.
neighbors.shared: you carry a light you didn't make, and you can tend it.

neighbors.heading: restless until
neighbors.text: Today a Guru told the restless mind: no one has found Him through cleverness. Paul wrote something close: "the world by wisdom knew not God." And Augustine prayed: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee."
neighbors.difference: In the Anand, rest comes through the True Guru and the Word, sung. For Christians, rest comes through Jesus, who said: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
neighbors.shared: a restless heart is looking for home, not a better argument.

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today Guru Amar Das told the restless mind that cleverness won't bring it home; rest comes through the Word. Muslims know that rest too. The Qur'an says: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" That remembrance, dhikr, is often a few sacred words repeated on prayer beads, again and again.
neighbors.difference: In the Anand, rest comes through the Guru's Word, sung in the sangat. For Muslims, dhikr remembers Allah in words from the Qur'an and the Prophet's practice.
neighbors.shared: a tired mind can rest in a word repeated with love.

neighbors.heading: pray without ceasing
neighbors.text: Today the remembering went on past the morning, sitting and standing, with every breath and bite. Catholics know that thread. Saint Paul wrote: "Pray without ceasing." Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite who worked in a monastery kitchen, said the clatter of pots didn't break his prayer; he kept God company at work as on his knees.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the thread is the Name, remembered through the Guru's Word. For Catholics, it is friendship with God in Christ, fed by the Mass and the Church's set prayers through the day.
neighbors.shared: prayer can ride along with the dishes.
neighbors.sources: 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (Douay-Rheims) · Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: walking, standing, sitting
neighbors.text: Today the remembering went on all day, sitting and standing, with every breath and mouthful. Buddhists practice something close. In a core teaching on mindfulness, the Buddha says to know it when walking, standing, sitting or lying down, and to be fully aware while eating and drinking. The breath is a place to come back to.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs remember the Name of the One through the day. Buddhist mindfulness attends to body, feelings and mind just as they are, as a path to freedom, not as remembrance of a God.
neighbors.shared: every breath and every bite is a chance to come back.

neighbors.heading: days as grass
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan asked, again and again, where is mother, where is father, and named what stays: remembrance of the Lord. A psalm walks the same line: "As for man, his days are as grass... For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone." Then it turns: "But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs meet passing with remembrance of the Name. Jews meet it with trust in God's lasting covenant love, and by remembering their dead, saying Kaddish and honoring parents as a commandment.
neighbors.shared: love your people fully; let something deeper hold the weight.

neighbors.heading: given back
neighbors.text: Today a verse asked where mother, father and children go, and named what doesn't pass. People on their own path ask too. The Stoic Epictetus taught: never say of anything, I have lost it, but, I have given it back. Marcus Aurelius wrote that time is a river of passing things, and its current is strong.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, what stays is remembrance of the Lord. The Stoics found steadiness in reason and in accepting nature's order; some spoke of God, but their calm rests on how we meet change.
neighbors.shared: hold your people close, and hold them lightly.

neighbors.heading: allah knoweth
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: what You do seems sweet to me. Muslims carry a close word. The Qur'an says: "it may happen that ye hate a thing which is good for you... Allah knoweth, ye know not." And a hadith marvels at the believer: thankful in good times, patient in harm, and both are good for them.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs speak of bhana, sweetly accepting the Lord's will while still standing against wrong. Muslims speak of patience and contentment with Allah's decree, alongside effort; trust never means doing nothing.
neighbors.shared: acceptance can be a calm place to stand, not giving up.

neighbors.heading: evenness is yoga
neighbors.text: Today a Guru called the Lord's doing sweet, and asked only for the Name. Hindus hear a close teaching in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna tells Arjuna to act, without clinging to results, and to stay even in success and failure. That evenness of mind, he says, is called yoga.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's evenness belongs to a path of action offered to God. Guru Arjan's sweetness is love for the One Lord's will, received through the Name, and Sikhs remember it alongside his own martyrdom.
neighbors.shared: a steady heart can meet the hard day.

neighbors.heading: the gift of no fear
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru called wise the one who frightens no one and fears no one. Buddhists know both halves. The Buddha taught that keeping the precepts, not killing, stealing or lying, is a great gift: freedom from fear for countless beings, and a share of that freedom for you. Many Buddha images raise an open palm, the gesture of no fear.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, fearlessness and no enmity echo qualities of the One named in the Mul Mantar. Buddhists ground them not in God but in ethical conduct and a mind freed by practice.
neighbors.shared: be someone others feel safe beside, and stand up anyway.
neighbors.sources: Abhisanda Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 8.39 (paraphrase) · the abhaya mudra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no fear in love
neighbors.text: Today a Guru joined two gifts: fear no one, and frighten no one. Christians find both in love. "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear," one letter says. Paul adds: "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour." And another letter: "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs see nirbhau and nirvair, without fear and without hate, as qualities of the One, lived out by the wise. Christians see fear cast out by God's love, made known in Christ.
neighbors.shared: the brave can also be gentle.

neighbors.heading: one great body
neighbors.text: Today the Guru listed the boxes people get sorted into, then said: recognize all humankind as one. People on their own path reach for the same line. The Stoic Seneca wrote that we are all limbs of one great body; nature made us kin, from the same source, and put love for one another in us.
neighbors.difference: The Guru grounds one human race in the One Creator, called both Karta and Karim. Seneca grounds it in nature and reason, a kinship anyone can hold, with or without belief in God.
neighbors.shared: under every label is a human being, like you.

neighbors.heading: of one, all mankind
neighbors.text: Today the tenth Guru named the boxes, Hindu, Muslim, Shia, Sunni, and said: recognize the whole human race as one. Catholics read Paul telling the Athenians that God "hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth." The Church teaches that all peoples form one community, with one origin and one final goal: God.
neighbors.difference: The Guru goes on to say the Creator and the Merciful are the same, across faiths. The Church honors what is true and holy in other religions, yet holds that the fullness of truth is found in Christ.
neighbors.shared: the boxes are real, and the people inside them are kin.

neighbors.heading: sparks from a blazing fire
neighbors.text: Today one fire threw off countless sparks that fell back into it. Hindus know this exact picture. The Mundaka Upanishad says that as sparks, like the fire itself, fly from a blazing fire by the thousand, so beings come forth from the Imperishable, and return there again.
neighbors.difference: Hindu schools read the sparks differently: some as finally one with Brahman, others as souls forever distinct. The Guru sets the image inside praise of the Timeless One, read by Sikhs through the Name.
neighbors.shared: you came from somewhere bright, and you belong to it.

neighbors.heading: one father
neighbors.text: Today sparks rose from one fire and fell back into it, all of it one. Jews ask from the same root: "Have we not all one father? Hath not one God created us?" The Mishnah adds that humanity began with one person, so that no one could say, my ancestor was greater than yours.
neighbors.difference: The Guru pictures beings rising from the One and merging back, like waves into water. In Judaism, the Creator stays distinct from creation, and the soul returns to its Maker.
neighbors.shared: one source means no one gets to say they're better.

neighbors.heading: who can be against us
neighbors.text: Today the tenth Guru, who had lost so much, wrote that no one can harm the one the Lord protects. Christians hear Paul: "If God be for us, who can be against us?" Paul had been beaten and jailed, and still wrote that neither death nor life could separate us from the love of God.
neighbors.difference: For the Guru, the Friend is the Timeless One, and his trust stood beside action for justice. For Christians, that unbreakable love is known in Christ, who suffered, died and rose.
neighbors.shared: what's held by love, no one can take.

neighbors.heading: our protecting friend
neighbors.text: Today the Guru wrote to an emperor: what can an enemy do when the Friend is kind? The Qur'an gives Muslims close words: "Naught befalleth us save that which Allah hath decreed for us. He is our protecting Friend." When believers were warned of a gathering army, they answered: "Allah is Sufficient for us!"
neighbors.difference: The Guru's Friend is the Timeless One, known through the Gurus' Word. For Muslims, Allah is the Protector, known through the Qur'an and the Prophet, and trust goes hand in hand with taking every sensible step.
neighbors.shared: being held doesn't mean you stop working.

neighbors.heading: in his own tongue
neighbors.text: Today the tenth Guru wrote in Persian, Punjabi and Braj, a language for each listener. Catholics remember Pentecost, when the apostles spoke and "every man heard them speak in his own tongue." Since the Second Vatican Council, Mass is usually said in local languages, while Latin remains the Church's own.
neighbors.difference: The Guru chose each language for its listeners, praising the Timeless One in all three. For Catholics, Pentecost is the Holy Spirit's gift to the Church, carrying one faith into every language.
neighbors.shared: speak so the listener hears it in their own words.

neighbors.heading: in your own language
neighbors.text: Today the Guru wrote in three languages so each listener could hear. Buddhists tell a story too. Two monks asked the Buddha to set his words in the learned Vedic style. He said no, and allowed his teaching to be learned in one's own language. It went on to live in Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan and more.
neighbors.difference: The Guru's many tongues all praise the Timeless One. For Buddhists, words are a raft toward awakening, not praise of a creator; scholars also read "own language" as the Buddha's own dialect.
neighbors.shared: the truth wants to be heard in your own words.
